title: Pure Land in the West
hookLine: Japanese American Buddhist churches and Chinese temples far from Asia

lines: A SIGN THAT READS BUDDHIST CHURCH.
cards: Paper lanterns are strung across a parking lot on a summer evening in California. Families in light cotton robes and sneakers move in a slow circle while a big drum keeps the time.
Behind them stands a plain building with a sign that reads Buddhist Church. On Sunday morning, people will sit in pews there and chant Namu Amida Butsu.
In another city, a Chinese temple wedged between a bakery and a dry cleaner has a red door, a cloud of incense, and the words Namo Amituofo by the entrance.
The teaching of the land of bliss crossed an ocean in the luggage of ordinary people. Today: Pure Land in the West.

teach.h: THE LAND IS IN THE WEST.
teach.b: First, the direction. The Pure Land sutras place Amitabha's land in the west. In the Smaller Sukhavati-vyuha, the Buddha tells Shariputra about a world far off to the west, called Sukhavati, where Amitabha teaches now.

Tradition says people faced the setting sun to remember it. Families from Japan and China moved east across the Pacific, and the West became a new home: Hawaii, California, Canada. Second, the buildings.

teach.h: TEMPLES THAT TOOK THE NAME CHURCH.
teach.b: Japanese immigrant families, among them Shin Buddhists, built temples in their new towns, and some of those temples took the name church.
They added pews, Sunday services, a Dharma school for the children, and songs in English beside the old chants. Some readers see that as giving something up.
Some members describe it the other way: the shape changed so the teaching could stay.
Third, what a temple did for people far from home.

It was a kitchen and a meal hall. It kept the old language alive for grandparents and taught it to grandchildren. It held funerals, weddings, and the summer Obon festival, where the dead are remembered with dancing.
Chinese temples did much the same, with chanting, vegetarian meals, and Amituofo said as a greeting and a thank-you. Fourth, why this teaching traveled so well. The nembutsu needs no building at all.
It fits inside one breath, in a kitchen in Ohio or a hospital room in Toronto: the one thing those families could carry without a crate or a ticket.

how: Japanese American Shin Buddhist temples, some called Buddhist churches, hold Sunday services with chanting of the nembutsu, Dharma school and a summer Obon festival; Chinese Pure Land temples outside Asia hold chanting services and use Amituofo as a greeting.

games.q: what does “pure land in the west” mean?
o: a Western school that replaced chanting with sermons
the Amitabha teaching carried to temples far from Asia
the belief that the land of bliss lies in Europe

games.q: Pure Land in the West: tap the pairs.
p: the land of bliss, far to the west
a temple with pews and Sunday services
the name, said in Chinese temples
a summer festival remembering the dead

s: Pure Land practice stayed in Asia
Japanese and Chinese families carried it to temples far away.
some Japanese American temples call themselves churches
they took the name and added pews, Sunday services and a Dharma school.
the nembutsu can only be said inside a temple
it fits inside one breath, in a kitchen or a hospital room.

games.q: you've just arrived in a new country with your family. there's no temple anywhere nearby. what happens to the practice?
o: it waits until you can go back home.
you say the name at home, and with neighbors you build a temple.
you keep it strictly private and never share it.
games.why: immigrant families said the name at home and built temples in their new towns, some of them called churches, so the teaching could stay.

practice: Picture a Pure Land temple: a plain room, a standing golden figure of Amida on the altar with one hand raised, incense rising, folding chairs or pews, somebody's grandmother bowing with her palms together.
If you say the nembutsu, say it once, softly; if not, just breathe and stay in that room for a while.

wordCard.voice: Pure Land in the West. The teaching of Amitabha's land, carried by Japanese and Chinese families to temples far from Asia, where the name is still said. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: jodo, pure land. it's the jodo in Jodo Shinshu, the Shin school of the Pure Land.

carryVoice: Your line: far from home. Go gently today, and I'll see you tomorrow.
